analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover over-the-counter birth control pills with no copay.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 89 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party, was referred to a House committee and its health subcommittee in July 2015 and died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the preventive-care coverage rules so health insurance plans and employer plans must cover over-the-counter daily birth control pills the way they already cover prescribed contraceptives — with no copay and no prescription required. It also states the House's view that drug makers should seek Food and Drug Administration approval to sell these pills without a prescription, and that retailers stocking them may not interfere with access. It was introduced in July 2015, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who use daily oral contraceptives, especially those who struggle with the cost or the hassle of getting a prescription. The bill's own findings cite a national survey finding that 1 in 3 women have struggled to afford birth control at some point, leading them to use it inconsistently [S3]. Once a pill is approved for over-the-counter sale, it could be bought without a doctor visit and billed to insurance with no out-of-pocket cost.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women who use birth control pills

how_it_helps.text: Requires health insurance and group health plans to cover over-the-counter daily oral contraceptives as preventive care for women, with no cost sharing, even without a prescription [S2][S3].

States the House's view that drug makers whose evidence supports it should apply to the FDA for approval to sell daily oral birth control without a prescription, and that the FDA should decide without delay if the product meets safety standards [S3].
Bars retailers that stock over-the-counter birth control from interfering with a customer's access to it or to accurate information about it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer health plans, through the added cost of covering a drug with no copay — a cost that flows back into premiums paid by all enrollees. Retailers stocking the pills would take on a new access obligation.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers, employer plans, and retailers

drawbacks.text: The coverage mandate adds to insurers' costs, and those costs flow into premiums paid by everyone with insurance, including people who do not use contraception [S3].

A good-faith objection: routing a cheap over-the-counter purchase through insurance can add administrative cost rather than save money, and some argue out-of-pocket affordability and insurance coverage are different problems that this bill merges into one mandate.

The bill does not itself approve any over-the-counter birth control — it only applies if and when the FDA approves one, and its call for drug makers to apply has no enforcement behind it, so its practical effect is contingent on decisions outside Congress [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For women who face cost or access barriers to birth control, the benefit is direct and concrete: no copay and no prescription requirement for a daily pill. The cost is modest and diffuse — slightly higher premiums spread across all insured people — and the bill leaves the FDA's role untouched. The bigger weakness is design contingency: nothing changes until a manufacturer wins FDA approval, and the bill can only pressure, not require, manufacturers to apply.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health Subcommittee in July 2015, and it sat there until the two-year Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Tammy Duckworth introduced the bill in the House on July 22, 2015 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and on July 24, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health [S5].
The bill drew 89 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican support [S4].
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — appears in the bill's action history before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the status quo, with no new coverage mandate. Women who struggle to afford birth control gained nothing; the cost and prescription barriers the bill targeted remained in place, and drug makers faced no new pressure to seek over-the-counter approval.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept the status quo

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral — took no action on the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 22, 2015 and never scheduled a markup or reported the bill.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health (Energy and Commerce)
against.role: Subcommittee of referral — took no action
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 24, 2015 and held no hearing or vote on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 90 original sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and none were Republicans; with Republicans holding the House majority and chairing the committee of referral, the bill never moved past the subcommittee referral.

industries.note: The bill would require plans to cover over-the-counter daily birth control with no cost sharing, adding to plan costs that flow into premiums. The industry's interest in avoiding the mandate runs against the women who would get free access.

The bill states the House's view that manufacturers should seek FDA approval to sell daily oral birth control over the counter, which would open a new non-prescription market, and that insurers would cover such products with no copay. The industry's expanded sales would come alongside the access gains the bill offers women.

Retailers stocking over-the-counter birth control could not interfere with customer access to it or to accurate information about it, a new obligation. The limitation section keeps the duty narrow, applying only to retailers that choose to stock the product.
